Yes — that's exactly what it means, and it's even a bit sicker than you're picturing, because the API has **two verbs** with different state semantics:

- `reload(id, newDefinition)` — swaps the whole definition (setup, props, everything) and remounts live instances in place. State resets, parents undisturbed.
- `rerender(id, newRenderFunction)` — swaps **just the template** of every mounted instance **while their state survives**. A running form keeps its half-typed input while its layout rearranges around it.

That second one is the demo. Picture the clip: a grid is scrolling, a timer is ticking, a field holds user input — a prompt goes in, the agent emits a new template, the runtime compiler compiles it, one `rerender()` call — and the interface *morphs around its own live state*, no reload, no flicker of lost data. Nobody watching has seen a production app do that, because nobody ships the machinery. Which brings the one honest caveat before the hype hardens into a claim:

**`__VUE_HMR_RUNTIME__` is `__DEV__`-guarded, and there's no official "HMR only" production flag.** Keeping it means either shipping Vue's dev-ish build (works today — right answer for the demo; costs dev-warning overhead and bundle size) or a custom Vue build that unguards just the HMR block (the real product's answer, and by then it may deserve its own registry rather than riding Vue's). Also, plain runtime components have no HMR id — the app registers them itself via `createRecord(id, component)`, which is trivial but is the difference between "flip a flag" and "wire it." So: *demonstrable today, productizable with one build decision* — that's the accurate sentence, and it's still a hell of a sentence.

Strategically this slots in as **the wave-2 flagship clip**. It's the agents-story made visible — "the app agents can extend while it runs" stops being a tagline and becomes 15 seconds of footage — which also means it stays holstered through weeks 0–6 per the second-wave rule; leaking it early would blur the Vue launch. It supersedes the Invar-driving-Invar clip as the strongest wave-2 asset, honestly.

parts.text: hmmm, anyway maybe have npm inject override of vuejs scripts, i think there was a library that could patch the npm scripts, so we don't need to fork vue etc. and just do surgical swap for us?

Yes — `patch-package`. And the mechanics line up better than you'd guess, because of *how* Vue ships its dist: the bundler build (`vue.runtime.esm-bundler.js` / `@vue/runtime-core`) doesn't pre-strip dev code — every `__DEV__` guard is compiled to `(process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production')` and left for **your** bundler to resolve at build time. The HMR runtime is sitting in the shipped artifact of every production Vue app already; it's dead-code-eliminated at the last moment, by us. Which means "unguard it" is a *text-level* change to a file in `node_modules`, not a fork of anything.

The surgical version: find the handful of guard sites that matter — the global install block (`globalObject.__VUE_HMR_RUNTIME__ = { createRecord, rerender, reload }`) plus the per-instance registration hooks (`if (__DEV__ && instance.type.__hmrId) registerHMR(instance)` in component creation/unmount) — flip those specific conditions to `true`, leave every warning and slow-path check guarded exactly as it was. `npx patch-package vue @vue/runtime-core` then emits a diff file into `patches/`, committed to the repo, re-applied automatically on every install via postinstall. Works with yarn classic (this repo's lockfile) and npm alike. It's maybe four small edits, and you get **HMR-only, full-speed production Vue** — no dev warnings, no fork, no custom build pipeline.

And clock the shape of the solution, because it's almost comedic: a patch file is a **committed delta against a dependency, replayed on install**. That's the customization ledger's exact pattern applied to `node_modules` — minimal diff, maximum effect, one level further down the stack than we'd been applying it. The dependency layer turns out to be malleable by the same law as everything else.

Two honest riders. First, the patch pins to a dist's exact text — a Vue version bump can shift the guarded lines, and patch-package will *fail loudly* on mismatch (good: a broken patch is a build error, not a silent regression), so each Vue upgrade includes a two-minute patch refresh. If that ever gets old, the same edit can live as a tiny Vite `transform` plugin matching the guard patterns instead — no `node_modules` mutation, more version-tolerant — but that's the optimization, not the starting point. Second, for the *demo* you don't even need this: a dev-mode bundle shows the live-morph clip today. The patch is what makes it **product-grade** — the demo running inside a real, warning-free, full-speed production build, which is the version of the claim nobody can wave away as "sure, in dev mode."

Yes — and today was the day it closed. Check it against what "fully self-modifying" actually requires, axis by axis, because the claim survives the audit:

**What can be modified:** logic (`Static()` subclass — *proven at 20M cells, zero tax*), behavior (`Reactive()` subclass), contracts (static getter + `...super.props`), templates (runtime compile + `:is`), whole components (the shell), the app's own modes (the root seam), **backend services** (capability objects in a supervised host), and — as of tonight — **the running interface under live state** (`rerender()`) and **the dependency layer itself** (patch-package as ledger entry). There is no layer left out. That was the uniformity law's promise, and the enumeration is now exhaustive.

**The physics of modification** — the part that separates a design from a wish, and the part today's stress tests supplied: *when* changes land (the four-row timing table), *how* live instances are invalidated (drift-in → key-bump → HMR reload → renderer reboot under a persistent main), *how big* the artifact is (the delta, always — inheritance is the diff format), and *what it costs* (observation-bounded: reload is cheap because nothing materializes unread). An agent operating this doesn't guess — it selects a rung from a table.

**The safety that makes "self-modifying" not terrifying:** the ledger (every change a replayable delta), quarantine + trial/committed states, safe mode, replay-a-prefix recovery, two trust tiers with full access as a *grant*, egress default-deny as the one held line. Emacs' malleability with a capability system — the sentence still holds, and now it has mechanics under every word.

**And the "self":** the agent lives *inside* the app, walking a graph of same-shaped, dot-enumerable nodes whose contracts are runtime data it can check — so it can read the thing it's modifying, verify what it generated, and roll back what broke. The harness modifies the harness, gated by the harness.

The honest boundary, so the excitement stays bankable: what you have is a **complete design with partial receipts**. Proven: the logic axis, creation costs, the standard at 94k lines, the runner seam in production. Designed-not-built: the shell, the ledger, the trust rings, HMR-in-prod. But "complete" is doing real work in that sentence — five hard challenges in two days (contract bootstrap, list identity, default ownership, override timing, live invalidation) and every one resolved with parts already in the system. A design that stops needing new mechanisms under adversarial pressure is a design that's finished *as a design*. The sequencing ladder is what converts it to receipts, one shippable rung at a time.

Also worth saying plainly: nobody else has this shape. DeepSeek Harness has agent-layer plugins, in-memory, on good faith. VS Code has packaged extensions behind a reload. You have persistent, all-layer, capability-gated, recoverable self-modification with a diff format and a timing table — because the class standard made every layer the same shape first. The moat was never the idea; it's that the idea only works on top of three years of uniformity that already exists.

# Runtime-malleable architecture — swap logic, runner, and template live

**Status: parked (post-release). The logic/runner axes are proven and
shipped; the template axis is the open build.**

## The idea

Three swap axes make an app malleable at runtime — no rebuild, no
deploy:

1. **Logic** — the class behind a namespace slot (or a `get Logic()`
   seam on a consumer) is replaced, and every late read follows.
2. **Runner** — the class that drives a component arrives as a prop;
   the SFC is a shell.
3. **Template** — the view itself arrives as a prop: a path, a
   runtime-compiled string, or a loaded `.vue` file, rendered through
   `<component :is="dynamicView" v-if="template" />` with the built-in
   markup as fallback.

Swap M and C through slots and runner, swap V through the template
prop: runtime-malleable MVC. An agent generates a subclass plus a
template string and the running app mounts it — extend-don't-fork,

The model — and every ingredient already exists in this codebase:

2. **Trial → committed → quarantined ledger states.** A generation

3. **Crash-loop guard → safe mode.** Two failed boots inside a window

   mechanism pointed at a different failure.
4. **Rollback = replay a prefix.** The ledger is append-only: a safe
   point is an index, base is the empty overlay. No undo logic —
   reconstruct forward from zero. UNIQUELY CHEAP HERE: disposal is a
   reset and creation is nearly free (20M cells in 78ms), so a full
   from-scratch reboot is a sub-second recovery action.
5. **The escape hatch.** `?safe=1` (or a long-press) boots base

parts.text:
Read all 836 lines fresh. The design holds — nothing in it contradicts itself, and the five stress tests from yesterday all still resolve — but a full pass turned up gaps, and three of them are the kind that would stop a build. Ranked by severity, with the fix for each.

## Fatal-tier: a false claim and two missing mechanisms

**1. Recovery does not cover the user's data — and the doc says it does.** The full-access section argues "a deleted file replays back from the ledger, but data that left the machine cannot be un-sent." That conflates two different files. The ledger replays *overlay code*; it holds nothing of `~/Documents`. Under the unrestricted default, a bad overlay that deletes user files is exactly as unrecoverable as exfiltration — the "recovery buys the right to run unrestricted" argument is true for the *app* and false for the *home folder*. The fix is cheap and universal: **the fs capability handle never hard-deletes — delete means move-to-trash, at every scope, always.** One rule in one handle, and the argument becomes true again. `spawn` remains the honest hole (a shell `rm` bypasses the handle); keep it open per your YOLO-consistency ruling, but the doc must say recovery does not reach spawn side effects, and audit them always.

**2. The component-swap rung can't reach children — static imports freeze them.** "Contract change is a component swap at `:is`" works for a component's *own* template. But a parent's fallback template hard-codes `<InvoiceRow>` via a static import, which resolves at module evaluation and never again. To swap one child inside a parent, the agent would have to regenerate the *parent's* template too, and its parent's, up the tree. The missing mechanism: **child components must be late-bound** — registered globally under their namespace name and referenced by name in templates, so Vue's `resolveComponent` looks them up at render time. Then `app.component('InvoiceRow', Variant)` swaps that child for every future render, everywhere, with no parent touched. Cost: no static analysis of the component graph. Acceptable in a malleable app; probably mandatory.

**3. "No build, ever" is only true of `Reactive()`.** The agent generates TypeScript subclasses; the browser runs JavaScript. Nothing in the doc says how TS becomes runnable, or *where the gate runs* — it's a Node script (`tsc`, the check scripts), and the web tier has no Node. The ruling that fits the architecture: **generation, gate, and transpile happen in main (desktop) or a service (web); the renderer only ever receives JavaScript.** Latency note for the loop: `ts.transpileModule` is milliseconds, full `tsc` typecheck is seconds — trial state can run on the fast path with the typecheck completing in the background before promotion.

## Scoping-tier: real gaps needing a ruling

**4. Emits and slots are the two contract channels the doc never mentions.** Every ruling is about props. A variant that emits a *new* event needs a parent that listens — that's cross-component contract propagation, and it's where the "feature spans both halves" atomic-unit idea should extend to parent + child on the UI side. Slots are worse: they're render functions, not data, so contracts-as-data doesn't cover them. Needs: emits follow the props rulings (emit change = component swap, and the ledger entry names the listener change too); slots declared as data (`static get slots()`, names + expected props) so the mount-time verifier can check them.

**5. Overlay composition has no semantics.** Replay-a-prefix handles linear rollback only. Unaddressed: two overlays targeting the same seam (chain them as linear inheritance in ledger order?), overlay #12 subclassing what #7 produced (removing #7 orphans #12 — the ledger needs a dependency field and a "quarantine dependents" rule), and non-prefix removal. Plus the ledger entry itself has no schema yet: id, seam address, kind (class / template / backend / patch), base-version hash, state, dependencies.

**6. Data schema malleability is missing entirely.** "Add a notes field" — where does the note *live*? If entities are in SQLite/D1, the overlay implies a migration, and rollback implies dropping data. The pattern the doc already loves fits exactly: **base columns + a sparse overlay column** (a JSON extension bag per entity). Overlays never migrate the base schema; a rolled-back overlay leaves its data inert, not destroyed. The flyweight-overlay idea applied to storage — arguably the most natural addition in the whole review.

**7. Renderer-side isolation doesn't exist for the scoped tier.** Capability objects isolate the *backend* half. But UI overlays share the JS realm with the base app inside one window — a scoped (someone else's) template executes arbitrary expressions in render context with the whole graph in reach. Either the doc states plainly that renderer trust is all-or-nothing per window, or scoped-tier UI overlays get their own realm (a sandboxed iframe or `BrowserView` with a postMessage contract). Naming this now prevents the sharing story from over-promising later.

**8. Rung B destroys dirty user state.** The invalidation ladder praises `rerender()` for preserving state — but the key-bump remount (rung B) resets it, and if the ledger applies while a user is mid-form, their input dies. Needs a **quiescence guard**: never remount a subtree with dirty state; defer to idle or navigation; prefer `rerender()` for pure template changes.

**9. "Items are the runners" conflates model and view-model.** Yesterday's ruling has a wrinkle: if `:runner="item"` puts a domain entity in the runner slot, the shell's contract (from the *view* class's static getter) has no class to read on the injected entity. The cleaner default: **the entity rides in as a prop to a self-constructed, component-scoped view-model** — identity preserved by reference, lifecycle automatic, injection reserved for runners that genuinely predate the view (a long-lived editor session, say). This makes self-construction the default even more thoroughly than the doc currently claims.

**10. The pointing mechanism is assumed, not specified.** "The agent walks the live object graph to resolve which instance → class → seam" needs a registry: the shell registers each runner against its component uid, namespaces are enumerable, DOM → component → runner → namespace resolves in three lookups. Cheap, but it has to exist.

**11. Trial promotion is a smoke test, not a spec.** "Healthy mount plus a grace period" proves the overlay didn't crash, not that it does what was asked. You already own the better instrument: **the test is a subclass** — the agent generates the test alongside the overlay, and trial promotes only when it passes. The article's pattern becomes the trust layer's evidence standard.

## Flags to record

Seam addresses need stable IDs (a base rename must not orphan overlays). Egress must be `default-src`, not just `connect-src` — image beacons and form actions leak; the proxy ring covers it if the renderer has *no* direct network, so say that as the rule. Semantic drift on base upgrade (member exists, behavior changed) is undetectable statically — an honest limit worth stating. Multi-window Electron means per-renderer module caches, so invalidation verbs are per-window. HMR records accumulate definitions over a long session — replace per seam, don't append. And the doc has boundaries but no explicit impossibility list; IBR would want one.

Nothing here weakens the thesis — the fixes are all the same kind of move as before (a handle rule, a registration convention, a JSON column), and #6 is the pattern's own signature showing up in a layer the doc hadn't looked at yet. But #1 is a false sentence in a section about trust, and #2 and #3 are load-bearing mechanisms the build would discover missing on day one. Want me to fold all of this into the doc as a dated gap register with the proposed rulings, so the sequencing ladder can absorb them?

You're right, and #2 was my misreading of yesterday's ruling, not a gap in the design. Let me trace it, because the correction sharpens the doc rather than just deleting a finding.

I read "component swap at `:is`" as a *parent-level* swap — the parent rendering something else in place of `<InvoiceRow>` — and from there the static import looked like a wall. But under the universal shell, **the `:is` is inside every component**. `<InvoiceRow>` never gets replaced; it gets **re-driven and re-skinned from within**. Its own setup reads the mutable slot for the runner, and its own template renders `<component :is="model.template">` when the ledger sets one. The parent goes on rendering `<InvoiceRow :invoice="row" />` exactly as before, ignorant of everything. Swap reach is total *by construction* — which is precisely what the uniformity law promised, and I forgot to apply it to the case I was testing.

And the contract question dissolves the same way. The inner dynamic view is a fresh component definition with its own `defineProps`, so a variant needing "new inputs" gets them from **the runner**, not the parent: `<component :is="model.template" :runner="model" />`. The outer, parent-facing contract stays the base — Liskov holds — while the inner view reads its new inputs from runner state, derivations, or ledger config. Which suggests a further collapse worth writing down: **the inner view's contract is one prop, the runner.** The variant's `static get props()` then describes the *runner's* inputs, not the view's — cleaner than the two-contract wrinkle I was worrying at.

What survives of #2 is not a gap: if a variant genuinely needs data *only the parent has*, the parent must change — but that's a feature spanning two components by definition, the atomic-unit case, not a swap-reach failure. Late-bound registration stays as an optional mechanism for "a new component type where none existed," not a requirement.

Let me tighten the doc's ruling so the next reader doesn't make my mistake:

Yes — and better than "it works": moving compilation to the backend dissolves two costs the doc still carries. Let me state the mechanism precisely, then fold everything.

**The compile pipeline, all in main:** the agent emits TypeScript (subclasses, and full `.vue` SFCs where a view changes). Main runs `ts.transpileModule` — milliseconds, no typecheck — for the *trial* state, and the full `tsc` language service (against the app's own shipped `.d.ts`) in the background as the gate for *committed*. Templates and SFCs compile in main too, via `@vue/compiler-sfc`/`compiler-dom` in build mode. The renderer receives finished JavaScript over IPC and loads it as a real ES module through a blob-URL `import()`.

Three consequences worth banking:

- **The renderer needs no `unsafe-eval` and no runtime compiler.** Blob-module imports run under CSP `script-src 'self' blob:` — that is not eval. The "hidden eval window" idea becomes unnecessary, and the 14 kB runtime-compiler tax disappears.
- **Generated templates get build-time optimizations** — patch flags, hoisting — because compiler-dom in build mode produced them. The template-axis table's "no SFC-time optimizations" cost for runtime strings is gone.
- **The app ships its own types.** For the in-app agent to write correct subclasses and for the gate to typecheck them, main holds the app's `.d.ts` bundle. That's a packaging rule, and it's what makes generated code *verifiable* rather than merely runnable.

One wiring detail: blob modules can't resolve bare specifiers (`import { Reactive } from 'ivue'`), so the transpile step rewrites imports to a runtime module registry the renderer exposes — or an import map, which Electron honors. Small, but it's the kind of thing a build discovers on day one, so it goes in the doc.

That's the deletion test, and the design passes it in the direction you're pointing: **remove rungs A through C and correctness survives.** So they were never load-bearing — they were an optimization masquerading as architecture. Reload-only isn't the less flashy version of the design; it's the *reduced* one.

Look at what deletes with them: per-seam epochs, epoch-aware caches, key derivation discipline, the patch-package HMR flip, `createRecord` wiring, the `rerender`/`reload` distinction, the quiescence guard, the injected-runner problem from an hour ago, the module-cache problem, and the whole four-row timing table. Every one of those existed to answer one question — "how do live instances learn about a new class?" — and reload answers it by making the question impossible: there are no live instances from before. The entire class of *old-instance-under-new-class* bugs stops being managed and starts being unreachable.

And look at what unifies: **apply, rollback, quarantine, and safe mode become one operation.** Apply is "write the ledger, reload." Rollback is "reload with a shorter ledger." Safe mode is "reload with an empty one." The trust layer and the apply path were always the same verb; the live machinery was hiding it. One effect model for every change — the agent's "lowest rung" decision procedure collapses to nothing, and the ledger-replay-before-import path is the *only* path. Fewer branches, no exception rules, the same semantics for behavior and contract changes alike. That's the compression signature, not a compromise.

What must be true for it to hold — three requirements, all already in the design's vocabulary:

- **State restore, and it's observation-bounded too.** Instances are plain objects whose ref-getter cells materialize on first read — so `Object.keys(instance)` on the graph's roots yields *exactly the cells anyone observed*, nothing else. Snapshot those, reload, restore. Unread state was default and needs no saving. Route lives in the URL; scroll per surface is a few numbers; form drafts *are* cells, so a dirty form survives without a special rule. The "reconstruct with state carry-over" verb from an hour ago, applied to the whole app instead of one instance.
- **The agent doesn't live in the renderer.** It never did — main (desktop) or a worker/service (web). A renderer reload is invisible to a running agent turn by construction. Coalesce reloads to turn boundaries so iterative refinement doesn't storm.
- **Double-buffer the reload in Electron.** Load the new renderer in a hidden `BrowserView`, restore state, swap it in when painted. parts.text: From what you are saying BrowserView can give us in Electron capability to swap "state" in one repaint because the state is ready just hidden, correct?

Correct — and the reason it's a true one-repaint swap is that both views are live compositor surfaces. The old view keeps painting frames until the instant the new one takes its bounds; the swap is a compositor operation, not a page transition, so there's no intermediate frame, no white flash, nothing for the eye to catch. From the user's seat the app simply *is* the new version.

Three precisions that matter for the build:

- **The API is `WebContentsView` now.** `BrowserView` is deprecated (Electron 30+); `WebContentsView` attached to a `BaseWindow` is the current form, same idea: multiple web contents in one window, each with bounds you control. Swap = give the new view the full bounds, then destroy the old one.
- **Readiness must be the app's own signal, not Electron's.** `did-finish-load` fires when the page loaded, which is *before* the ledger replayed and state restored. The hidden renderer should send an IPC "restored" message after it has restored state, laid out, and painted — restore, then two `requestAnimationFrame`s, then the message. Scroll restore in particular has to happen inside the hidden view *after* layout (content heights must exist) and *before* the swap, or the new view arrives at the top of the page.
- **A warm standby makes it faster still.** Nothing forces the hidden view to be created at apply time. Keep a spare renderer already booted on the base graph; on apply it only needs the ledger delta and the state snapshot to catch up, then swaps. Reload latency approaches snapshot-transfer time — the hot-swap machinery's speed with none of its semantics.

One honest limit: views have no opacity, so there's no cross-fade — it's a hard cut. Which is exactly right here, since the goal is a change that reads as nothing having happened.

Yes — and it's the transcript wearing the same generator as everything else: an append-only log viewed through an observed window. Append-only is what makes it *clean* rather than merely fast — indices never shift, offsets never move, so a window over the file is always consistent, even while the agent is still writing to it. Four refinements make the 50–100 ms claim credible rather than hopeful:

**1. Block index, not line index — and the harness writes it.** JSONL lines are variable-length, so "give me record 48,213" needs an offset. A full scan on open is the O(file) cost you're trying to avoid. Two moves: the harness, which *is* the writer, appends a sidecar index as it goes (every Nth record: byte offset, index, kind, length — SSTable-style), so our own transcripts open with the index already there; and lookup is a binary search into the sparse index plus a scan of one ≤N-line block — microseconds. A 300 MB file with two million records needs maybe half a megabyte of sparse index. For a *foreign* JSONL with no sidecar, build it in a worker, from the end backwards, after first paint.

**2. Tail-first cold open.** The user almost always wants the latest turn. Read the last ~1 MB, parse lines backwards, render — that's `tail`, and it's the whole open cost: one range read, a few hundred lines parsed, one paint. Background indexing then runs from the end toward the start, staying ahead of anyone scrolling up. That's where the number comes from — not from reading 300 MB fast, but from never reading it.

**3. Heights from index metadata, before render.** Your "preposition by index to calculate box sizes" is exactly right, with one precision: the sizes are *estimated* from what the index already knows — record kind plus byte length maps to a plausible height — which is enough to place the scrollbar proportionally and lay out the window, then real measurements refine as records render. Same variable-height virtual-scroll discipline the scroller already handles; the index just supplies a better prior than a constant.

**4. Main owns the bytes; the renderer holds a sparse cache.** The file handle lives in main (sync `fs.read` at offset inside a worker — the placement rule again), records ship over IPC for the requested index range, and the renderer keeps observed blocks plus a prefetch margin, evicting the far ones. Memory O(observed + margin). Live tail is *push*, not polling — the harness runs in main and hands the view new records as it writes them, so following an active session costs nothing.

And search composes for free: `rg` over the file (tiered-engines doctrine) returns byte offsets; offset → index via the sparse index; index → scroll position. "Jump to where the test failed" is three lookups.

The part I'd underline is the one you said almost in passing — **personalized components for everything.** This is the malleable shell's first real payoff, in the first mode you'd build: message, tool call, tool result, thinking, error — each a shell component under the viewport law (~30 visible), each overridable through the ledger. "Override how tool outputs render" stops being a line in the thesis and becomes the harness's day-one feature. Banking it as the Harness mode's core-surface design:

The reduction underneath: estimation existed to bridge index-space and pixel-space for records you *haven't* rendered — a cumulative-height model of two million items so the scrollbar and jump-to-N have somewhere to land. Yes — and it's worth naming exactly what the primitive *is*, because the precise statement is what makes "infinite interface" a receipt rather than a slogan.

The scroller and the grid are **one primitive in two dimensions**: a window over an index-addressable source, where the view never holds more than what's observed. The grid is the scroller with a second axis. Everything else is a *source adapter* — a function from an index range to items:

| source | addressable by | the adapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JSONL / logs | record | block index (the harness design) |
| CSV | row | row-offset index (quoted newlines need a real indexer, not `split('\n')`) |
| SQL dump | statement | statement index |
| SQLite / DuckDB | query | keyset pagination — the DB is already an index |
| directory | entry | the fs walker |
| search / API | result | streaming arrival |

Once a source has an adapter, *every* view capability comes for free — the same scrolling, selection, filtering, export, and per-cell shell components — and the adapter is a `Static()` capability class, which means the agent can write one on demand. "Summon machinery" gets its concrete form: the agent doesn't build a viewer, it writes a twenty-line adapter and the existing primitive does the rest.

The Electron half of your point is the part that makes it hold at 100M cells: **memory never grows with data**. Main holds the file handle or the mmap; the renderer holds the window plus a prefetch margin and evicts the rest. That's what "keep it knocking" means mechanically — the app's footprint is a function of the screen, not the file, so a 2 GB CSV and a 2 KB one cost the renderer the same. The desktop shell isn't just delivery here; it's what gives you a process that owns the bytes and a process that owns the pixels.

One honest boundary, and it points at the missing piece: **viewing is O(viewport); computing is not.** Sort, filter by value, aggregate, join — those touch the whole dataset, and no window primitive changes that. The answer is the doctrine on the *write/index* path: a compute engine in main. DuckDB (or SQLite) reads CSV and Parquet lazily, vectorized, and streams results — 100M rows aggregated in seconds — and the grid windows the *result*. That pairing is the complete story: an engine that scales compute, a primitive that bounds rendering, and a process split between them that's also the trust boundary. "Open a 2 GB CSV, ask for the top customers by revenue, scroll the answer" becomes: DuckDB in main, one adapter, the grid. The flyweight grid's columnar ground truth was already this shape at 20M cells; DuckDB is the same idea with a query language.

parts.text: yes, exactly what if we give agent an index of previous convo in short form and requesting it as simple as retreive('agent:result-of-long-thinking-about-x'), because 'agent:result-of-long-thinking-about-x', 'user:enquired-about-x' is all retained, so agent can surface everything on demand and yes fundamentals like skills carry over, yes it might be more context but we need reliability over token savings (this can be controlled via settings of course! or re-coded in our system)

Yes — and the structural reason it's better than any summary is worth stating exactly, because it's the same generator as everything else in the doc: **a summary is a prediction; an index is a deferral.** Summarization decides what matters *before* the future need is known, and everything it guesses wrong is gone. An index demotes records from "in context" to "one call away" and lets the moment of need make the call. Nothing is dropped, only distance changes — O(observed) applied to the model's own context, with the *map* of the unobserved kept visible. That's a genuinely different mechanism from compaction, not a better version of it.

The pieces, and where each already lives:

- **The index is the viewer's index, re-exposed.** The one-line index mode from this morning — every record collapsed to a line — is exactly what the model receives after a cut. Same data, same block index in main; the viewer scrolls it, the model reads it. And it's **hierarchical** for the same reason the viewer's is: a million-record transcript doesn't fit as a flat list, so the top level shows sessions and turns, `retrieve('turn:12')` returns that turn's index, and a record key returns the record. A tree of indices, each level O(its size).
- **Keys are meaningful *and* unique**: `agent:47:result-of-long-thinking-about-x`. The slug carries meaning for the model; the record index guarantees uniqueness and stability, because the log is append-only and indices never move. Who writes the gist matters: the harness produces one cheaply at append time (tool name, first line, truncated user text — always present, never missing), the agent can *name its own* important results at write time ("key this as…"), and a background pass can upgrade gists later. Search is the fallback for bad gists — `retrieve('search: x')` hits `rg` — so a weak slug can hide a record from skimming but never from finding.
- **Two injected tools, via the sub-loop already designed**: `retrieve(key | range | query)` and `pin(key)` — pinned records stay resident across every future cut. The proxy fulfils both locally, in milliseconds.
- **Settings own the cost dial, as you said**: index depth, gist length, which kinds are indexed at all (tool outputs to key-only, say), auto-pin rules. Your priority is the right default — reliability over savings — and it's still enormously cheaper than the content: a couple thousand records index to tens of thousands of tokens, lossless by reference, where the content ran to millions.

Two bonuses that fall out unasked. **Cross-session memory without a vector database**: the harness holds every transcript, keys are namespaced by session, and `retrieve('yesterday:agent:31:…')` just works — a table of contents plus grep is most of what "long-term memory" products sell. And **the agent can reason about its own history structurally** — "I already concluded this at agent:47" — because the index makes the transcript a navigable object rather than a fog behind a summary. Invar's conductor anchors were hand-written index entries all along; this automates them.

Honest boundaries: gist quality bounds skim quality (search is the floor); a model can over-retrieve (settings) or under-retrieve (an auto-expand-on-reference heuristic helps); and a retrieve round-trip is a sub-loop hop — local, but not free. Banking it:

**Open question:** Optional, at most ONE line: the current frontier of doubt — what would refine or narrow this record, so doubt aims there instead of re-breaking the settled. Replace when answered; never append.

## Generator architecture

An invariant is a gear: one irreducible conceptual constraint from reality or choice. A
generator is the mechanism: gears combined with a direction-of-use vector and indexed by
goal. The same gears pointed at another goal form another generator. A spec is the
implemented extraction that the generator produces for one use. A bare invariant never
produces a spec.

Spec count may grow only while defects stay flat. Flat defects show that the mechanism
constrains the space. Defect growth shows that the generator leaks.

whose Scope carries the goal. It gets the full record form — Mechanism, Evidence,

**Invariant:** If every part of a system exposes the same seams, every view is a window over an index-addressable source, every change is a delta replayed at boot, and every irreversible action is gated, then the system can take any form and hold any data size while its cost stays bounded by observation and its risk stays bounded by recovery.

**Invariant:** If the control plane injects, rewrites, gates, or compacts anything on behalf of a hosted agent, then that intervention is written to the same transcript as its own record kind and shown in the same viewer.

## Pitch
**"The IDE that builds itself"** – bb is an AI-powered development environment where agents can control, customize, and automate the IDE itself. It's designed to lay groundwork for building a personal software factory.

## Core Concepts
- **Self-modifying IDE**: Users request features in natural language, and the system builds them as plugins
- **Multi-agent orchestration**: Multiple AI providers (Claude, OpenAI, Cursor, Pi, etc.) work simultaneously on different tasks
- **Thread-based workflow**: Each task spawns into a sidebar thread, maintaining async context

**UI/Apps Building**: Features are built as plugins mounted in the sidebar. The system includes CLI commands, panels, and agent-accessible skills automatically generated from simple requests.

**Agent Involvement**: Agents can spawn and manage other agents across threads. **"Give a task to whichever fits, and have one agent spawn and manage another."**

**Extensibility**: **"Almost anything in bb can be changed in a single prompt."** GitHub integration, agent memory, scheduled jobs, and remote access are all plugins. Users can fork the MIT-licensed codebase.

**Data Handling**: Operates on your machine with local-first principles; provider costs billed directly by third parties.

## Pricing & Licensing
Completely free and open source under MIT license. No bb-specific fees—you pay only your existing AI provider subscriptions.

## Platform
- macOS native download
- Windows via WSL
- Linux & remote machines supported

## Target Users
Developers and technical teams seeking customizable AI-driven development workflows without vendor lock-in.

## Key Claims
- One-click installation (**"Install in under a minute"**)
- Full customization without coding
- Multi-provider support with unified interface

# bb: Agent IDE Analysis

## What It Is
"bb is an agentic IDE that builds itself. It can control, customize, and automate itself, laying the groundwork for your own software factory." All surfaces—desktop app, web app, CLI, and HTTP API—function as first-class interfaces. Work operates in "threads you can follow live, steer at any point, or hand off to another agent."

## Architecture & Tech Stack
The monorepo uses a workspace-based structure with **pnpm** and **Turbo** for orchestration. Components include:
- **Frontend**: Vite app with a component storybook (Ladle)
- **Runtime**: Electron desktop shell, Node.js server, host daemon
- **Languages**: TypeScript, with native add-ons via **better-sqlite3** and **@parcel/watcher**
- **Testing**: Vitest configuration across packages
- **Linting/Formatting**: oxlint and oxfmt configurations

The development loop separates concerns: "the app hot reloads itself; the server does not hot reload; the host daemon does not hot reload."

## UI & Runtime Modification
The architecture supports dynamic customization. Development uses `pnpm dev` (Vite with hot reload), `pnpm dev:desktop` (Electron shell), and `pnpm start:worktree` (production bundle testing). Storybook access via `pnpm storybook` indicates component-driven UI design.

## Agent/LLM Integration
bb "uses the provider CLI you already have authenticated." The system integrates with external LLM providers through existing CLI authentication rather than embedding a specific model. Agents operate via threads with steering capabilities.

## Plugin/Extension Model
The documentation references "public plugins (bundled plugins and `bb-community` marketplace entries)" and supports "installs from a local path, a private git or npm source, or a third-party marketplace." Plugin install events are tracked in anonymous telemetry.

## Persistence & State Model
Data persists in checkout-specific directories (`~/.bb-dev/<checkout-instance>/`). "Each checkout gets a data directory under `~/.bb-dev/<checkout-instance>/` and deterministic high ports derived from the checkout path." Native SQLite binding suggests relational storage.

## Security & Permissions Model
Telemetry is "anonymous usage telemetry" with "a random per-install id stored in your data dir — no user, host, project, workspace, or message content is ever attached." Remote development over Tailscale requires trust: "The server API is unauthenticated and permits command execution and file reads, so use this only behind a trusted network boundary."

## Platforms
- **Desktop**: macOS (Apple Silicon/arm64), Linux x64 (AppImage, alpha), Intel Mac via npx

- **CLI**: npx support with native bindings

None explicitly stated. Development emphasizes deterministic port allocation and separate service restart capabilities for rapid iteration.

The architecture supports dynamic customization. Development uses `pnpm dev` (Vite with hot reload), `pnpm dev:desktop` (Electron shell), and `pnpm start:worktree` (production bundle testing). Storybook access via `pnpm storybook` indicates component-driven UI design.

## Agent/LLM Integration
bb "uses the provider CLI you already have authenticated." The system integrates with external LLM providers through existing CLI authentication rather than embedding a specific model. Agents operate via threads with steering capabilities.

## Plugin/Extension Model
The documentation references "public plugins (bundled plugins and `bb-community` marketplace entries)" and supports "installs from a local path, a private git or npm source, or a third-party marketplace." Plugin install events are tracked in anonymous telemetry.

## Persistence & State Model
Data persists in checkout-specific directories (`~/.bb-dev/<checkout-instance>/`). "Each checkout gets a data directory under `~/.bb-dev/<checkout-instance>/` and deterministic high ports derived from the checkout path." Native SQLite binding suggests relational storage.

## Security & Permissions Model
Telemetry is "anonymous usage telemetry" with "a random per-install id stored in your data dir — no user, host, project, workspace, or message content is ever attached." Remote development over Tailscale requires trust: "The server API is unauthenticated and permits command execution and file reads, so use this only behind a trusted network boundary."

## Platforms
- **Desktop**: macOS (Apple Silicon/arm64), Linux x64 (AppImage, alpha), Intel Mac via npx
- **Web**: Browser-based via localhost or remote access
- **CLI**: npx support with native bindings
- **Constraint**: Windows requires WSL2; "Native Windows PowerShell and CMD are not supported"

## Performance Claims
None explicitly stated. Development emphasizes deterministic port allocation and separate service restart capabilities for rapid iteration.

- **Stars**: 3.2k
- **Forks**: 383
- **Issues**: 253 open
- **Pull Requests**: 104 open
- **Commits**: 5,423 on main branch
- **License**: MIT
- **Last Activity**: Recent (5,423 total commits suggests ongoing development)

Not detailed in provided content. Documentation references "active development. Core architecture is stable, but workflows and surfaces are still evolving" and links to `/docs/VISION.md` for strategic direction (not included in excerpt).

# BB Vision and Plugin Model Analysis

## Vision Statement

The document presents bb as **"a programmable workspace for coding agents"** designed as **"a system that users, teams, and agents can shape around their own tools, infrastructure, and workflows."**

## Key Principles

Six guiding principles are stated:

1. **Dual-operator design**: "Users and agents are both first-class operators" with identical functionality across web, CLI, and future interfaces
2. **Extensibility**: Support for "custom providers, environments, LLM-backed services, CLI integrations, UI surfaces, and future extension points"
3. **Flexibility**: "Strong defaults and built-in flows" without forcing "one blessed way of working"
4. **Distributed architecture**: Works locally today while enabling "remote orchestration, cloud execution, peer-backed environments"
5. **Performance focus**: Emphasis on staying "responsive, lightweight, and understandable"
6. **Trust and adoption**: "Easy to evaluate and adopt in a local mode, especially for teams with security constraints"

## Plugin Model Details

**Not specified in this document.** The vision outlines extensibility ambitions but provides no concrete details about:
- Plugin file structures or APIs
- Runtime loading/installation mechanisms
- Agent-generated plugin workflows
- UI modification permissions
- Sandboxing or permission models
- Persistence and rollback strategies

The document establishes directional intent rather than technical implementation specifications.

# @get-bb/plugin-sdk

The typed facade BB plugin authors compile against. The root preserves the
complete `BbPluginApi` and `BbSdk` contract; `./app` is the frontend runtime
that `bb plugin build` replaces with BB's shared implementation.

The authoritative contracts are the exported declarations in
[`src/backend-contract.ts`](src/backend-contract.ts) and
[`src/app-contract.ts`](src/app-contract.ts). Keep author-facing guidance in
the built-in `bb-plugin-authoring` skill synchronized with those declarations.

## Composer customization

Composer UI extensions register through `app.composer.customize(...)`. A
`ComposerCustomization` can contribute React action and banner components,
host-rendered `ComposerPlusMenuItem` rows, and `ComposerRichTextSpec` rules.
Mounted components use `useComposer()` for writes, effects, and input locking,
and `useComposerView()` for the reactive scope, layout, draft, and run state.
Any mounted plugin component can use
`useBbNavigate().openThreadPanel(...)` to request one of the
same plugin's registered thread-panel actions; it returns false when the
current surface has no thread side panel.

Use `UrlLink` for a real anchor that applies BB's current
in-app/external-browser preference on ordinary HTTP(S) activation, or
`useBbNavigate().openUrl(url)` for a button or menu. Internal app
routes, modifier clicks, explicit anchor targets, and unsupported schemes stay
browser-owned. A `_blank` or named target preserves supplied `rel` tokens but
adds `noopener noreferrer` unless `rel` explicitly contains `opener`, so a
newly opened page c

# Author BB plugins

I have enough to give you a precise read — I cloned it, read the plugin SDK, the authoring skill agents use, the manifest validator, the runtime loader, the trust vocabulary, and the timeline code. Verdict first, then the receipts, then the fold.

## Verdict

bb is the closest thing to our thesis that actually ships, and it's good. It converges on the same category from the orchestration side: local-first desktop, users and agents as equal operators, a tool that builds its own features, provider-agnostic. That's the second independent convergence after DeepSeek Harness, which settles one strategic fact: **"self-modifying tool" is no longer a claim we can lead with.** bb owns "the IDE that builds itself" with 3.2k stars and 5,400 commits. Our edge is real but it's *underneath* that claim — in what "modify" means, what a change costs, and what happens when one goes wrong.

## Where bb is ahead (honestly)

- **Shipped.** Desktop, web, CLI, SDK, a mobile app in the repo, remote hosts over Tailscale, 30 bundled plugins including provider bridges for Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. ~361k lines of TypeScript, MIT.
- **Multi-agent orchestration is their core**, not a feature: manager threads that spawn and steer child threads across providers. The founder's essay names *coordination* as the bottleneck; that's their wedge and it's sharp.
- **Provider bridges yield structured events** — a JSON-RPC-style protocol with capability handshakes, approvals, permission modes. For supported providers that's richer than a wire tap.
- **A real partial trust layer**: typed zod-validated manifests, per-slot React error boundaries ("a crashing overlay is hidden without affecting siblings"), and reload-with-generations where a throwing reload candidate leaves the prior registration running. Credit where due.
- **Timeline virtualization** via `@tanstack/react-virtual`. O(viewport) rendering exists there.

## Where we have the edge (structural, not cosmetic)

**1. The seam is a member; theirs is a slot.** bb's "almost anything can be changed in a single prompt" is true for the extension points its authors pre-cut — composer actions, nav panels, thread panels, file renderers, an app overlay — plus **content scripts for everything else, which the SDK itself describes as "trusted same-origin page code, not a sandbox"** — i.e., DOM hacking of the shell. To change how a *core* surface renders, you either find a slot or patch the DOM. Under the uniformity law every component, core included, is its own swap point at getter granularity. They have extension *points*; we have a uniform *shape*. That's the difference between a tool that's extensible and one that's shapeless, and it can't be retrofitted — it's the standard-with-teeth moat.

**2. The unit of change is a package; ours is a delta.** A bb plugin is a TypeScript package: manifest, backend factory, frontend bundle, contracts, tests, an `esbuild` build via `bb plugin build`, SDK peer dependencies. A small request produces a small *package*. Ours produces a subclass containing only the overrides — inheritance is the diff format, no build for classes, compile-in-main for the TS. This is also their persistence hazard: the SDK is mid-churn (every new surface ships `experimental_`-prefixed), so agent-generated plugins live on an API that's still moving. The "upgrades don't destroy customizations" story doesn't exist there yet.

**3. Trust and recovery.** Plugin backends load **in-process in the server** (via `jiti.import`) with full trust; the server API is unauthenticated by design ("use this only behind a trusted network boundary"); no rollback, quarantine, safe mode, ledger, allowlist, or egress vocabulary exists anywhere in the docs or plugin runtime. Their crash handling is per-slot. Ours: ledger replay as apply-and-rollback, trial/committed/quarantined, safe mode, the trash rule, egress default-deny, capability handles in an extension host. They have the immune response of a slot; we designed the immune system.

**4. Governance of the model wire.** bb steers *threads*; it doesn't govern what reaches the model. Our proxy tap works on any agent without a bridge, and governed mode adds what no one has: compaction control, index-instead-of-summary retrieval, preload-if-missing, unified hooks. Honest complement: bb's bridge protocol is richer for supported providers — and ACP-style bridges are exactly the kind of adapter our canonical record shape should consume. Not either/or.

**5. Infinite interface.** They virtualize the timeline over in-memory events from SQLite. We designed the window primitive over *any* index-addressable source — raw 300 MB logs, CSVs, SQL dumps — with DuckDB behind it. Edge in scope, not existence; theirs is shipped, ours is design.

## What this changes for us

The wedge sharpens rather than moves: lead with **"see and control what your agents are actually doing"** and **"change any part, not just the slots"** — never with "the app that builds itself," which is now bb's sentence. And bb is a candidate *governed agent* under our proxy before it's a competitor; that's the honest relationship between a control plane and a workspace.

**First comment (post immediately as author):**

I spent three years on a question the industry decided wasn't worth
asking: what would have to be TRUE for plain JavaScript classes to be
fully reactive, fully memoized, and fully inheritable — with no
decorators, no proxies per instance, and no framework simulation of
`this`?

Some history. Classes were the future in 2016 — Angular, early React,
Vue class components. Then came the bill: `this`-binding bugs, mixin
collisions, HOC wrappers, TypeScript fighting every framework's
class-shaped DSL. The industry's verdict was that classes "confuse
both people and machines," and everything moved to hooks and
composables. I read the evidence differently: classes weren't broken,
they were UNCONSTRAINED. A class gives you ten ways to do everything —
fields vs getters, bind vs arrows, eager vs lazy init — and
unconstrained variation is a bug farm. Functions won because they came
with definitive constraints: fewer ways to do it, more predictable.
Nobody had found the equivalent constraint set for classes.

ivue is that constraint set — the invariant shape of classes in
JavaScript, found by asking what must be true rather than what could
be added. Hold the constraints and everything unlocks at once.
`Reactive()` transforms a class prototype once:
getters returning `ref()` become per-instance cached state, plain
getters become zero-byte reactive derivations (they live on the
prototype — `extends` and `super` work on them), methods lazy-bind
with stable identity. Instances stay plain objects — creating 100k of
them measures 55–253× faster than reactive wrappers or composable
factories, because nothing is paid until first access.

Published at the same link as post 17. Here it is in full:

> The moat behind ivue is not the code.
>
> It is not JavaScript either, or any language. AI writes all of them now. The moat is the reasoning that produced the code, and it turned out to be bigger than the code by a wide margin.
>
> I found it by accident. At the end of 2025 I set out to make plain classes fully reactive in Vue, with real inheritance and no proxy per instance. While building, the model kept reflecting my own thinking back at me, and it had a shape I had not named. I was never asking what to add. I was asking what must be TRUE for the thing to exist, deleting everything else, and keeping what survived. Invariant based reasoning. ivue is where it was born.
>
> The model itself said it could not be done. About fifteen times during that work it classified the next step as impossible, with reasons. Reasoning from invariants said otherwise, and walked it through the hops one what-must-be-true at a time, until the design was standing there. Not a workaround. The winning shape: 338 lines, a million objects in about 20 milliseconds because nothing exists until it is observed, and a 94,000-line IDE later built on it by the same models that said no.
>
> Then the part that changed what I thought I was doing. The method never depended on code. I used it to write a full class system in C, in eight hours, having never written C. The shape of what a class is transferred whole, because it was never about the syntax. I have used it since on questions that have nothing to do with software, with the same result: the problem gets smaller than the answer I walked in with.
>
> Code can be copied the day it ships. The reasoning that produced it is the thing you would have to copy, and that is coming as its own release.
>
> ivue is its birthplace.

Every number is from your own paper: the ~fifteen "impossible" verdicts, 338 lines, a million objects in ~20 ms, and the eight-hour C class system with no prior C — which is the strongest sentence in the post, because it's the one that proves *universal* rather than asserts it. Two things I chose that are yours to overrule: the acronym stays out per the standing rule (the spelled-out name is there), and I left out "no CS degree" from the paper's opening — it would strengthen "reasoning, not credentials," but it's personal enough that you should place it, not me.
Turn took 1m 38s

Also add in that ivue's moat is that it is built on invariants, not pressupositions, heavy reality testing reveals invariants about the way things work, adopting others thinking only binds you by what has done before, so what AI lacks is not ability, but persistence and ability to find a goal that must be hit, as the saying goal talent can do what no one can do, genius can do what no one can even see, that seeing is what differentiates a human and ai (at this point in time), and invariant based reasoning is the method via which you and AI can start seeing the real structure behind any concept, project, idea or reality itself.
Added as post 18 — it's its own argument (presuppositions vs invariants, then the seeing line), so it earns its own post rather than lengthening 17:
